data.question: Should we adopt the rule change block_k 3 → 2 even though B and C voted against it, raise the constitutional floor invariants.min_company_on_time_rate from 0.60 to 0.65, or keep the current rules (v1)?
data.background: Proposal 1 passed check and the constitution and improved on_time_deliveries by +9.2 on 5/5 seeds, but B and C voted it down, so it failed the agreement gate. Overriding or renegotiating a failed company vote is a decision between human parties that I should not make. R1 changes a value in the constitution, and regulation changes always need a human decision, even though the current rules already meet the new floor.

options.summary: Lower blocking_guard threshold block_k from 3 to 2. Measured: on-time 131.0 (current 121.8, +9.2, improved on 5/5 seeds), late 1.2 (current 10.4), blocked s 985 (current 2404), lowest on-time rate 0.98 (current 0.84), unfinished 0.0, and KPI conditions met. Road violations rise to 34.0 (current 25.8). Adopting it means overriding the votes of B and C (votes ○ × ×).
options.stakeholders: Gains: customers of all companies, because late deliveries fall from 10.4 to 1.2 and the worst company's on-time rate rises to 0.98. Company A also gains (utility 38.4 → 45.4). Losses: Company C (utility 28.8 → 19.0) and, slightly, Company B (38.9 → 37.2). Both voted against it, so overriding them may hurt trust in the voting process. Other road users may be affected by more road violations (25.8 → 34.0).

options.summary: Raise the constitutional floor invariants.min_company_on_time_rate from 0.60 to 0.65. The current rules (lowest on-time rate 0.84) already meet it, so nothing changes in operation now. It only blocks future changes that would let the worst company fall below 0.65. The floor is still well below the KPI condition of 0.8.
options.stakeholders: Gains: customers of whichever company is worst off, because they get stronger protection against being kept waiting badly. This matches the KPI clause on fairness. Companies: no immediate cost. It slightly narrows the rule changes they can propose later. No customer loses in the short term.

options.summary: No change, stay at v1. Measured: on-time 121.8, late 10.4, blocked s 2404, road violations 25.8, lowest on-time rate 0.84, unfinished 0.0. Utility is 38.4 / 38.9 / 28.8.
options.stakeholders: Companies B and C keep their current utility. Customers forgo the measured gains from proposal 1 (+9.2 on-time deliveries, about 9 fewer late deliveries). The constitutional floor stays at 0.60.

recommendation.reason: R1 is low-risk: the current rules (0.84) and proposal 1 (0.98) both satisfy it. It strengthens the KPI's fairness clause without overriding anyone. Proposal 1 has the strongest measured KPI gain, but it failed the company vote, cuts C's utility by about a third, and raises road violations. I suggest not forcing it now. Instead, take it to B and C for negotiation, for example by investigating why C's utility falls while its on-time rate rises, or by pairing it with compensation, and re-measure before deciding.

unknowns: Why C's utility drops sharply (28.8 → 19.0) under proposal 1 while the lowest company on-time rate rises to 0.98; the utility components were not broken down.
What the extra road violations under proposal 1 (25.8 → 34.0) consist of, and whether they create safety risks.
Whether B and C would accept proposal 1 with compensation or a modified threshold, and how the companies would change their behaviour if it were forced through.
How customers perceive the current lateness (10.4 late deliveries) and whether they would notice the improvement.
Demand in the next period; results are averaged over only 5 seeds at the current demand level.
Whether overriding a failed company vote is acceptable under the town's governance norms.
